passage:
"You didn't even take your shoes off," Irawati said. "Sarika, what happened?"
"Same as always. Dilip sir sent another 'quick' task at seven. Thirty of those this week. Nobody says thanks, they just send the next one."
"You've been like this every Sunday night."
"I know. I dread Monday like a dentist appointment. I don't even care about the project any more." Sarika kicked her bag. "I feel bitter, and that's not who I am."
"So what will you do? Not just carry it and be a martyr."
"Talk to him. Show him the list. Ask what can wait." Sarika breathed out. "And take the leave days I've been hoarding."
"I'll pack snacks for the trip."

qa.q: How many quick tasks did Sarika say had arrived that week?
qa.a: Sarika said thirty of them had arrived that week.

qa.q: What does Sarika's dread of Monday, like a dentist appointment, reveal?
qa.a: It shows exhaustion and bitterness. Sarika no longer cares about the project and feels this is not the person Sarika wants to be.

qa.q: What plan did Sarika settle on?
qa.a: To talk to Dilip sir with the list of tasks, ask what can wait, and take the leave days.

qa.q: How does Irawati see Sarika carrying it all quietly?
qa.a: Irawati worries it will turn into silent martyrdom, so asks what Sarika will actually do about it.

grounding: Endless deadlines without thanks breed bitterness and Sunday dread; mature action is talking to the manager about load and taking leave.
